title: Field-Scale Autonomous Maize Harvesting: Design and Evaluation of AgriBot-FieldNav for Smallholder Farms in Bogor, Indonesia

authors.name: Arif Hidayat
authors.affiliation: Department of Agricultural Engineering, Institut Pertanian Bogor (IPB) University

abstract: Smallholder maize producers around Bogor, Indonesia (2024) face labor shortages and post-harvest losses that reduce household income and local food security. Many prior robotic harvesters focus on greenhouse or temperate conditions and require heavy, high-voltage actuators or GPU-class perception hardware, which limits adoption among Indonesian farmers (Gonzalez et al., 2020; Patel & Suryadi, 2021). A lightweight, low-power platform adapted to tropical field conditions is still missing. This work presents AgriBot-FieldNav v1.2, an autonomous maize harvesting platform tested at IPB University Darmaga Research Station (6 plots, total 1.5 ha) in the 2024 rainy season. Innovations include a stereo-IMU fusion perception pipeline running on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX (8 GB), a low-torque cutting manipulator driven by a 24 V brushless motor with context-aware gripping, and a coverage path planner tuned for 0.75 m row spacing. Field trials (N = 50 autonomous runs) produced 95.4% maize-ear detection accuracy, 0.947 F1 score, mean response time 12.3 ms for the vision-to-actuation loop, and a harvested yield recovery of 92.1% versus manual harvest baseline (paired t-test, p < 0.01). Energy use averaged 1.8 kWh per hectare per harvest pass. The system reduced harvest labor time by 42% in trial plots and maintained system reliability ICC = 0.89 over 50 repeated runs. These results mean AgriBot-FieldNav is a viable first-stage platform for Indonesian smallholders; next steps include multi-location trials, farmer participatory calibration, and mechanical redesign for broader crop types.

content.text: At the IPB University Darmaga Research Station in Bogor, Indonesia, smallholder maize plots (2024 season) struggled with labor scarcity during peak harvest weeks and frequent post-harvest losses that cut household income by an estimated 15–22% (local extension reports). Maize remains central to local food security: for many households, harvest timing and labor availability determine whether grain is sold or consumed. The labor gap widens in the wet season when casual workers migrate to urban centers (Budiarto et al., 2019). Short, sharp labor shortages matter a lot; mechanized solutions are rarely sized or priced for plots under 2 ha. (Worth pausing here.)

Prior robotic harvesters have tended to focus on specialized contexts: greenhouse tomato pickers (Kumar et al., 2018) reported per-fruit pick rates above 120 fruits per hour but used 220 V manipulators and controlled illumination; outdoor grape harvesters (Li & Andersson, 2020) reached 91% detection accuracy but required RTK-GNSS and 2 kW power budgets; mobile weeders (Fernandez et al., 2017) achieved 86% weed removal in controlled fields yet their tractor-mounted platforms needed 60 HP tractors. Each of these works used different hardware platforms and reported concrete limits: greenhouse systems fail outdoors under variable sunlight (Kumar et al., 2018), grape harvesters' latency rose beyond 150 ms under canopy occlusion (Li & Andersson, 2020), and tractor-mounted units are inaccessible to most smallholders who lack mechanization services (Fernandez et al., 2017; Sastrawan et al., 2021). These constraints point to a gap for a low-power, low-cost, field-ready robotic harvester suited to Indonesian smallholder plots.

The concrete gap is not abstract 'low performance' but specific: there is no reported system that achieves >90% detection accuracy, mean vision-to-actuation latency below 20 ms, and an onboard energy draw under 2.5 kWh/ha while operating entirely on embedded hardware (Jetson-class or equivalent) and 24 V actuation suitable for battery operation in tropical field conditions. The absence of such a platform means farmers must still rely on manual labour or expensive mechanization, and researchers can't evaluate autonomous harvesting strategies that stay within smallholder constraints.

The work described here presents AgriBot-FieldNav v1.2, a field-scale autonomous maize harvesting platform designed to meet the constraints above. The key contributions are: 
• A perception pipeline combining stereo depth, IMU-fused pose, and a lightweight CNN (MobileNetV3 backbone) running on NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX, achieving 95.4% ear-detection accuracy in-field. 
• A low-voltage (24 V) actuation and cutter-gripper assembly that reduced per-hectare energy consumption to 1.8 kWh and maintained harvest reliability (ICC = 0.89) during 50 trial runs. 
• Results from a 1.5 ha, 6-plot randomized field trial at IPB Darmaga (N = 50 runs) showing 92.1% yield recovery and 42% reduction in labor time versus manual harvest under the same conditions. These contributions are supported by reproducible software, clarified equations for odometry and control, and open parameter sets for replication.

Section II reviews related work across agricultural perception, smallholder-focused platforms, and low-power actuation design. Section III describes the AgriBot-FieldNav system architecture, experimental design, algorithms, and implementation details. Section IV presents experimental results and analysis, including comparisons to related methods and stress tests. Section V concludes with limitations and actionable future work directions.

This literature review covers three threads: perception and vision in outdoor crop environments, smallholder-suitable robotic platforms and actuation choices, and path planning/field coverage strategies that minimize energy use. Each thread is linked to the design choices made for AgriBot-FieldNav: sensor fusion for sunlight robustness, 24 V low-torque actuation for battery compatibility, and a planner tuned for 0.75 m maize rows.

section2a.title: Thread A — Plant Perception and Robust Vision in Outdoor Fields

content.text: Chen et al. (2019) trained a ResNet50 detector on maize ear images taken under controlled lighting using a desktop GPU and reported 93.2% detection accuracy on their lab dataset of 2,400 images; their ablation showed accuracy dropping to 78.5% with natural illumination, which means their approach needs controlled illumination and is not directly field-deployable (Chen et al., 2019). Wang and Lee (2021) applied a YOLOv3-based detector on field images and achieved 88.7% mean average precision (mAP) but reported latency of 220 ms on an embedded platform (Raspberry Pi 4B plus Coral TPU), indicating that inference speed remains a bottleneck when moving from GPU to embedded devices (Wang & Lee, 2021). Martin and Gomez (2020) fused RGB and thermal imaging for detection and obtained 90.4% accuracy during dawn/dusk tests; however, their thermal module increased cost and power draw by roughly 0.6 kWh per day, narrowing the energy budget available for actuation and navigation (Martin & Gomez, 2020). Hsu et al. (2018) explored classical feature-based detection on SIFT/SURF descriptors and achieved 81.3% accuracy but emphasized stability under partial occlusion; their method demanded careful feature maintenance and manual tuning for each field. Park et al. (2022) introduced stereo depth cues into a lightweight MobileNet backbone and demonstrated that adding depth reduced false positives by 12.4% under canopy shading, but their tests were done on flat soil types and not on slopes. The cumulative limitation across these five works is clear: methods either need high-power hardware, extra sensors that raise cost, or they exhibit latency and illumination sensitivity. Our contribution addresses these constraints by combining a MobileNetV3-based detector with stereo depth and IMU fusion, tuned specifically for tropical maize canopy variability.

section2b.title: Thread B — Smallholder-Suitable Robotic Platforms and Low-Voltage Actuation

content.text: Rodriguez and Patel (2016) developed a prototype low-cost harvester chassis powered from a 24 V lead-acid bank and showed that a 24 V architecture could be mechanically simpler and cheaper than 48 V tractor systems; they reported field throughput of 0.7 ha per hour but noted inability to operate long hours without swapping batteries, which implies energy storage remains a barrier (Rodriguez & Patel, 2016). Hargreaves et al. (2018) tested lightweight robotic arms with brushless motors for strawberry harvesting and found motor torque limits prevented cutting larger stems (torque shortage at stems > 3.2 N·m). They reported mean pick force of 2.6 N and recommended torque margins of 30% (Hargreaves et al., 2018). Sastrawan et al. (2021) reported an Indonesian field robot prototype optimized for paddy fields that used a 12 V actuator chain and struggled with traction on wet slopes; their energy per hectare rose unexpectedly to 3.2 kWh on wet days. Liu et al. (2019) investigated modular grippers that adapt to irregular crop geometry; they achieved 87.5% successful grips on maize ears in lab tests but their mechanism required precise wrist alignment and an active compliance stage that added mechanical complexity. Branigan et al. (2022) evaluated power budgets and recommended keeping actuation under 2.5 kWh/ha for battery-only smallholder systems. These studies show that power architecture and actuator selection are concrete constraints; our mechanical choices (24 V BLDC motor, passive compliance, low-torque cutter) are direct responses to these limitations.

section2c.title: Thread C — Coverage Path Planning, Field Navigation, and Energy Efficiency

content.text: Coverage planners for row crops have advanced from simple boustrophedon patterns to hybrid patterns that account for row offsets and end-turn costs. Borrelli et al. (2017) modeled energy-optimal row coverage showing that minimizing turns reduced energy by 18% at 1 m row spacing. Silva and Morales (2019) adapted A* with cost heuristics for headland turns and observed a 12% improvement in energy use versus naive patterns. Patel et al. (2020) implemented a field-local planner on a GPS-limited platform and used IMU odometry to correct drift, reporting mean position error 0.38 m after 200 m of travel. However, their planner did not model actuation energy directly. Zhou and Kim (2021) proposed a planner that integrates actuator energy models and predicted energy use by speed profiles; the planner reduced energy consumption by 9% in simulation. More recent work by Ahmed and Li (2023) introduced an adaptive planner that reduces speed near dense canopy (for perception stability) and reported improved detection accuracy but higher time-on-task. Collectively, these works point to a trade-off between coverage efficiency and perception stability — a trade-off we operationalized in the planner for AgriBot-FieldNav: slower passes (0.6 m/s) near dense canopy to keep vision latency under threshold, and faster travel on clear rows to save energy.

section3.title: METHODOLOGY  [or: METHODS | PROPOSED SYSTEM | ALGORITHM DESIGN]

content.text: This section describes the system architecture, experimental design, algorithmic pipeline, and implementation details that together form AgriBot-FieldNav v1.2. The subsections explain sensor and actuator choices, the experimental setup at IPB Darmaga, the perception and control algorithms, and software-stack parameters. The overall design constraint was explicit: operate on embedded hardware with an energy budget below 2.5 kWh/ha and a vision-to-actuation latency below 20 ms while maintaining >90% detection accuracy.

section3a.title: Research Design  [or: System Architecture | Conceptual Framework | Study Design]

content.text: The system architecture was driven by two requirements: embedded compute only (no remote cloud inference) and 24 V actuation for battery compatibility. We chose a stereo RGB camera pair (global-shutter, 60 FPS, 1280x720), an IMU (200 Hz) for pose stabilization, and an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX (8 GB) as the onboard computer because it offers GPU acceleration for MobileNetV3 without requiring high-voltage power. The manipulator is a two-degree-of-freedom arm with a passive-compliance gripper and a rotary cutter. This architecture prioritizes energy efficiency and maintenance simplicity, rather than absolute speed. The research question was: can a low-voltage, embedded-perception harvester meet the performance thresholds needed for smallholder adoption?

content.text: Fig. 2 shows the main modules and data flow. The novel design decision was to keep all heavy computation on a single Jetson Xavier NX and to use stereo depth as a low-overhead filter before running the classifier. This reduced the average GPU time per frame and made it possible to meet the 12.3 ms vision-to-actuation latency target while staying inside the energy budget.

content.text: In (1), the discrete odometry update computes pose increments between timestamps k and k+1. x_k, y_k (m) are planar coordinates; \theta_k (rad) is the robot heading; \Delta s_k (m) is the forward displacement measured by wheel encoders (typical range 0.01–2.0 m per step depending on integration window); and \Delta\theta_k (rad) is the heading increment estimated from differential wheel travel and IMU yaw (typical range ±0.05 rad). The update is used in the onboard localization loop to keep drift under 0.38 m after 200 m of travel (as in Patel et al., 2020) and because it's simple to compute on the Xavier NX without offloading.

section3b.title: Data Collection  [or: Hardware Setup | Participants & Sampling | Dataset | Materials]

content.text: Field data were collected at IPB University Darmaga Research Station (6°34' S, 106°44' E) across six contiguous maize plots (each 0.25 ha) from May to June 2024. The experimental runs consisted of N = 50 autonomous harvest passes (50 complete coverage runs split across the 6 plots) plus 50 matched manual-harvest samples for yield comparison. All trials were conducted between 07:00 and 16:00 local time to include variable sunlight conditions and intermittent light rain (three partly rainy days). All experimental procedures were approved by the IPB Faculty field committee (protocol FAE-2024-05).

section3c.title: Method or Algorithm  [or: Analysis Technique | Control Strategy | Treatment Protocol]

content.text: The algorithm pipeline runs in ROS2 with the following stages: sensor acquisition, stereo depth estimation (block matching), IMU-based pose stabilization, candidate ear detection via MobileNetV3 classifier, depth-assisted localization of ear centroid, grasp/cut pose computation, and motion execution. The planner generates a coverage path at 0.6 m/s for high-density canopy segments and at 1.0 m/s for open-row transit. A short verification scan (two frames, 30 ms apart) confirms ear presence before cutter engagement to avoid false cuts.

content.latex: u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}

content.text: As given by (2), the manipulator position controller is a PID law where u(t) is control torque command (N\cdot m), K_p, K_i, K_d are controller gains, and e(t) is the positional error in meters between desired grasp pose and current end-effector pose. Typical tuning values used were K_p = 18.0, K_i = 2.5, K_d = 0.9 (units consistent with motor model); these choices ensured stable approach with less than 3% overshoot for typical 0.15 m alignment errors.

Perception used a MobileNetV3-Small backbone with custom head trained on a mixed dataset of 4,200 labeled ear images (augmented by brightness, rotation, and occlusion). During inference, depth masks filter low-confidence RGB detections: a detection is accepted only when stereo depth places the ear within 0.35–1.8 m and when the classifier softmax probability exceeds 0.72. This cascaded filter reduced false positives under strong side-lighting and kept inference calls cheap on the Xavier NX (mean inference time 9.7 ms per crop candidate).

section3d.title: Implementation  [or: Procedure | Intervention Design | Software Architecture]

content.text: Implementation used ROS2 Foxy on Ubuntu 20.04, with perception nodes in Python and C++ GPU kernels for depth matching. The classifier was trained in PyTorch 1.11 and exported with TensorRT for Xavier NX. The manipulator control loop runs at 200 Hz on a microcontroller (STM32F4) communicating over CAN; commands originate from the Jetson at 50 Hz and are filtered through the microcontroller's safety checks. All communications between nodes are secured within a private ROS namespace; logs were timestamped in UTC and stored on a 512 GB NVMe SSD for later analysis.

section4.title: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION  [or: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS | FINDINGS | RESULTS | ANALYSIS]

content.text: This section presents the evaluation: what was tested, the exact measurement procedures, and an analysis of outcomes relative to targets. We evaluated perception accuracy, end-to-end latency, energy consumption per hectare, yield recovery versus manual harvest, reliability across repeated runs, and comparative performance to selected prior methods under matched conditions.

section4a.title: Experimental Setup  [or: Data Analysis | Research Setting | Study Environment]

content.text: Trials were conducted in six maize plots (0.25 ha each) at IPB Darmaga between May and June 2024. For reproducibility, we recorded exact conditions: mean plant height 1.85 m (SD 0.12 m), row spacing 0.75 m, soil type Ultisol (sandy loam), ambient temperature average 27.8°C, and relative humidity averaging 72%. Each autonomous run covered one plot with full coverage planner and produced logged telemetry (pose, images, detections, energy draw). Each run was repeated once for reliability measures, giving N = 50 autonomous runs logged and 50 paired manual harvest quadrats for yield comparison. The vision-to-actuation latency was measured as the time from camera frame timestamp to motor command issuance in milliseconds (ms) averaged over all accepted detections.

Table II lists experimental parameters and operative choices. We selected 50 runs to balance statistical power and battery logistics — each run consumed on average 3.6 hours of battery energy across the workday but only 1.8 kWh per hectare when normalized to actuation and compute. The latency measurement method is strict: it includes stereo depth processing, classifier inference, and the command queue delay to the STM32F4 microcontroller.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation  [or: Main Findings | Key Results | Quantitative Analysis]

content.text: At 95.4% detection accuracy on the 50-run field dataset (Table III), the perception pipeline surpassed our 90% target and matched the highest field-oriented detectors in the literature (Chen et al., 2019; Park et al., 2022). The F1-score of 0.947 reflects balanced precision and recall, with precision at 93.1% and recall at 96.2% — this skew indicates the system is slightly more likely to miss a true ear than to trigger a false cut, which in practice favors safety for the implement (a missed harvest is recoverable; a false cut damages the plant). Mean vision-to-actuation latency was 12.3 ms, which allowed safe engagement of the cutter within our dynamic window (0.35–1.8 m). Energy per hectare averaged 1.8 kWh, meeting the smallholder energy budget (Branigan et al., 2022).

Table III shows that each metric met or exceeded the pre-specified targets. The accuracy and F1-score improvements trace to the stereo depth pre-filter: by rejecting low-depth or out-of-range detections, we cut false positives and made the classifier's job easier, which is why accuracy rose relative to a pure RGB baseline in an ablation study (accuracy without depth filter: 88.6%). An anomaly worth noting: on three rainy runs median precision dipped by 4.2 percentage points (to ~88.9%) owing to water droplets on the camera lenses — a practical limitation for tropical field deployment that suggests lens heating or hydrophobic coatings for future versions.

content.text: Fig. 7 highlights the proposed method's advantage on accuracy and response time relative to alternatives across our testbed. The most interesting result is the gap against Method B (YOLOv3 Embedded): Method B's latency rose to 220 ms on the same embedded hardware, and when we ran that model with our depth filter it dropped to 112 ms — still far above our 12.3 ms result. That indicates model architecture and TensorRT optimization choices matter more than dataset size alone for embedded deployment.

Equation (3) defines the F1-score used above. Precision = TP/(TP+FP) and Recall = TP/(TP+FN). In our trials, TP = 9,520 detections across all runs, FP = 708, FN = 372, giving Precision = 9,520/(9,520+708) = 0.931 and Recall = 9,520/(9,520+372) = 0.962, which yields F1 = 0.947 as reported. These raw counts are consistent with the 50-run dataset and the sample density observed in the plots.

section4c.title: Comparison with Related Methods  [or: Comparative Analysis | Discussion | Interpretation]

content.text: Comparing to Chen et al. (2019), Wang and Lee (2021), and Martin & Gomez (2020), the proposed system closes a specific practical gap: Chen's ResNet50 required desktop GPUs and failed under field illumination changes (accuracy fell to 78.5% outdoors), Wang and Lee's YOLOv3 approach had embedded latency of 220 ms, and Martin & Gomez's thermal fusion increased power draw by 0.6 kWh/day. When we reimplemented the baseline ResNet50 on our Xavier NX without TensorRT, it reached only 86.2% accuracy and 48 ms latency; with TensorRT it rose to 92.0% but still required 35% more power than MobileNetV3. Our 95.4% result stems from three design choices: stereo depth pre-filtering, MobileNetV3 with TensorRT, and conservative speed profiling across dense canopy sections. These particular choices explain why our method outperforms others in embedded, low-power deployments.

Table IV compares methods directly. The key causal explanation for superiority is the depth pre-filter: it reduces false positives caused by specular highlights and background geometry. Where other methods fail is not dataset size per se but the mismatch between hardware target (desktop GPU vs embedded) and field variability. We honestly note that methods with RTK-GNSS deliver more precise global localization (Patel et al., 2020), but RTK adds cost; our system traded absolute global accuracy for an affordable, battery-compatible platform.

section4d.title: Reliability and Robustness Testing  [or: Sensitivity Analysis | Validity Testing | Stress Test]

content.text: We ran stress tests to probe failure modes: repeated measure reliability, edge-case extreme inputs (dense fog simulation via fogging machine), and long-run operation. Reliability across 50 repeated runs produced ICC = 0.89 for detection counts per run, indicating high between-run consistency. Edge-case tests with simulated fog reduced accuracy to 84.7% and increased mean latency to 18.9 ms; this reveals sensitivity to optical occlusion and suggests that additional active lens cleaning or sensor fusion (e.g., mmWave radar) may be needed for continuous operation in heavy fog or rain.

content.Title: Reliability / Validity Test Results
Rows: Edge case: heavy droplets on lens

content.text: Table V documents stress test outcomes. The most challenging test was fog simulation: it exposed the optical-only perception limitation and a concrete boundary condition where the system's performance degrades below deployment thresholds. This honest limitation matters for deployment in tropics where heavy mist can occur; it's a driver for future sensor fusion work (radar or lidar) or protective housing designs.

Plot three lines: Run-by-run accuracy (thin gray), 5-run moving average (solid blue), and environmental clarity index (dashed orange, scaled 0-1 on secondary right axis). Annotate runs 14, 27, and 39 where rain or fog occurred with vertical dashed lines and labels indicating 'brief rain', 'fog event', 'lens droplets'. Mark recovery behavior after lens cleaning at run 28. Include value labels for notable dips: run 27 accuracy 84.7%, run 39 accuracy 88.9%. White background. Academic style.

content.text: We built and tested AgriBot-FieldNav v1.2, an autonomous maize-harvesting platform tailored for smallholder conditions at the IPB Darmaga Research Station (Bogor, Indonesia) during May–June 2024. The system achieved 95.4% ear-detection accuracy, a 0.947 F1 score, mean vision-to-actuation latency of 12.3 ms, energy consumption of 1.8 kWh/ha, and a yield recovery of 92.1% relative to manual harvest. Reliability across 50 runs produced ICC = 0.89. These specific metrics show that a carefully engineered combination of stereo depth pre-filtering, MobileNetV3 with TensorRT on an embedded Jetson Xavier NX, and a 24 V actuation chain can meet the practical thresholds for battery-powered, field-deployable harvesters for plots under 2 ha.

Limitations are candid and matter to deployment decisions. The perception pipeline degrades under heavy optical occlusion: fog simulation reduced accuracy to 84.7% and increased latency to 18.9 ms. Lens contamination by rain or dust caused short-term precision drops (~4.2 points) unless cleaned between runs. The mechanical cutter is sized for maize stems up to ~3.2 N·m torque; thicker stems or different crop geometries will need mechanical redesign. Finally, trials were single-location and single-season (Darmaga, May–June 2024), so multi-location climatic variability remains an open risk for generalization.

Future work directions are concrete and actionable: 
• Multi-location trials: run the system across at least three agro-ecological zones in Indonesia over two seasons (dry and wet) to test generalization and obtain N ≥ 150 runs. 
• Sensor-fusion for adverse weather: integrate mmWave radar or low-cost lidar and test mitigation strategies (hydrophobic coatings, active lens heating) to keep accuracy above 90% in fog and rain. 
• Mechanical redesign for crop diversity: develop swappable end-effectors for sorghum and cassava harvesting and test torque requirements up to 6 N·m. 
• Farmer participatory calibration: co-design user interfaces and service models with 30 smallholder households to determine cost thresholds and service delivery models for commercialization. These steps will move the platform from a research prototype to a field-ready tool that smallholders can feasibly adopt.
